rules.text:
[precautionary] Sequence any step that shrinks, simplifies, deletes, or otherwise minimizes code strictly after a correctness check, and re-run that check against the result before treating the step as done. A simplification that has not been re-validated is not finished, no matter how much smaller or cleaner it looks.
Falsification: this pattern is confirmed only inside one of four tested agentic bug-fix configurations (SWE-bench patch refinement); if gated vs. ungated deletion stops paying off on refactoring or long-horizon tasks, treat this as a property of patch-style fixes, not of simplification generally.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a shrinking/deleting change is proposed, merged, or presented as complete without the correctness check (test suite or equivalent) having been re-run against the post-change state. SATISFIES if the check runs after the change and its result is what the step's completion rests on.
rules.evidence: RECAP's Oracle-Guided Refinement mode — the one deployment mode that subordinates the conciseness/refinement step to a mechanical test-pass gate — recovered and exceeded baseline resolution across SWE-agent, while unconditional (ungated) minimal-patch prompting and trained minimizers cost resolved instances relative to baseline across all four tested host agents (Agentless, SWE-agent, Moatless, OpenHands). Called 'the best-evidenced finding in the study' in the exploration document (Direction 6). Scope note carried forward honestly: the underlying benchmark is patch-refinement/bug-fixing, and the document's own falsification test for this direction flags refactoring and long-horizon agentic tasks as unconfirmed transfer — the mechanism (gate before finishing, not after) is what generalizes, not a specific magnitude.
rules.audit_note: The rule is tagged "grounded" but its own claimed-evidence paragraph discloses the disqualifying caveat: OGR's win is one of four tested SWE-bench host-agent configurations (Agentless, SWE-agent, Moatless, OpenHands lost or were the losing baseline set; only SWE-agent's OGR run beat baseline), the domain is narrow automated patch-refinement/bug-fixing, and the exploration doc's own Challenge note for this exact direction (line 302) says transfer to "agentic refactoring or long-horizon tasks" is unconfirmed and the falsification test is to check whether the gate still pays off there. The rule text is written with no such scope — "any step that shrinks, simplifies, deletes, or otherwise minimizes code" — which reaches straight into the unconfirmed territory (refactoring, general code shrinking) that the source explicitly flags as untested. Tagging that as "grounded" is the over-tagging failure the audit is watching for: the evidence grounds the mechanism inside one narrow, single-configuration benchmark, not the rule's actual scope. This is also, per the exploration doc, "the best-evidenced finding in the study" and one of only 15/15 directions that "came back weakened" under challenge — i.e. even the strongest direction in the corpus doesn't clear "grounded" once its own falsification test is applied.

rules.text: Apply the identical correctness re-check to additions and to deletions alike. Neither direction carries a special burden — growing the code and shrinking it both stand or fall on the same post-change check, not on a narrative about which one is more suspicious or which one needs more justification.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a rule, review process, or prompt demands justification, extra scrutiny, or a higher bar for a deletion that an equivalent addition would not face (or vice versa). SATISFIES if additions and deletions are held to the same correctness re-check and nothing else.
rules.evidence: RECAP's gate mechanism re-validates whatever patch came out of refinement regardless of whether it grew or shrank the diff — it does not itself privilege deletions for extra scrutiny. The exploration document's challenge round found that treating deletion as the specially-suspect direction (its Direction 7) 'converts [the evidence] into an asymmetric preservation prior that could entrench exactly the bloat the rest of the document is about,' and that framing was evaluated and rejected in favor of the symmetric one (locked decision).
rules.audit_note:
The rule text is fine and correctly implements the locked SYMMETRIC GATE decision (no magnitude, transfers cleanly since RECAP is an agentic-coding/SWE-bench study, rests on no [!!] claim). The defect is the AUTHOR'S STATUS tag: "precautionary" overclaims the evidentiary footing by one tier.

The author's own caveat already concedes "no study directly compares a symmetric gate against an asymmetric one in this setting" — the falsification test was designed, not run. More decisively, the exploration doc's own Irreducible-tension note (2026-09-10-simplicity.md:278) states plainly that "the corpus does not adjudicate which framing should be a skill's default posture, and the choice of default is most of what a skill *is*" — both the symmetric-gate framing and Direction 7's asymmetric "deletion needs justification" framing read the *same* RECAP and linter-reward evidence (line 278: "Both read the same RECAP and linter-reward evidence — one emphasising the destructive failure mode... the other the corrective success mode"). The Challenge round's rejection of Direction 7 (line 303, cited as CLAIMED EVIDENCE) is itself a reasoned argument about which failure mode to guard against, not a finding that adjudicates the tie.

This project's own established definition of the tag (skills/writing-scannable-prose/evidence-and-limits.md:7, sibling skill by the same author) draws the line precisely: "`precautionary` means the check rests on convergence across related findings rather than a single settled result." G2 doesn't rest on convergence toward *this specific claim* (symmetry) — the D2-3 findings converge on "an unconditional push in one direction without a correctness gate costs resolved instances," which argues for having a gate at all, not for that gate being direction-blind. Whether the gate should additionally impose asymmetric scrutiny is exactly the question the corpus is silent on, per the exploration doc's own admission. That is a design choice dressed as evidentiary convergence — the textbook profile of `judgment`, not `precautionary`, under this project's own taxonomy.

Practical effect of the mistag: a reader trusts "precautionary" as resting on some (even indirect) empirical convergence pointing toward symmetry specifically. It doesn't — it rests on a mechanical-gate design argument that the exploration doc itself flags as irreducible/undecided by evidence. Ship the rule (it does not violate any locked decision — SYMMETRIC GATE is itself the locked decision, and G2 correctly encodes it), but retag it `judgment` so the skill isn't claiming more empirical footing for the *symmetry choice specifically* than the corpus provides.

rules.text:
Let only the correctness re-check block, accept, or reject a change. A simplicity signal — shorter, fewer files, fewer branches, framed as 'more minimal' — may inform which candidate to prefer among ones that already pass the correctness check, but it must never itself be the thing that decides pass or fail. This is a design default, not a measured result outside automated bug-fix patch-refinement: the evidence is strongest for that narrow setting and is extended here on the strength of that setting's own result, not on a demonstrated transfer.
Falsification: the evidence is a linter-reward RL loop on small code-generation models plus SWE-bench patch refinement; if letting a simplicity signal decide pass/fail outperforms confining it to a preference among already-passing candidates in a setting that has a working correctness check, treat this as a property of reward shaping in training rather than of review.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a change is rejected, blocked, or sent back on the stated grounds that it isn't simple or minimal enough while the correctness check passes. SATISFIES if the stated blocking reason is the correctness check's result and nothing else.
rules.evidence: In an RL training loop for small code-generation models, a Ruff-linter-based reward used as the dominant signal degraded functional correctness (pass@1 fell); the same reward subordinated to a unit-test gate beat test-only on both correctness and quality. RECAP's unconditional minimal-patch prompting and trained minimizers cost resolved instances relative to the test-gated mode. Corroborating practitioner report: on the most-shared anti-over-engineering prompt thread, appending 'minimum viable functionality' — making minimality itself the operative instruction rather than a preference among already-correct outputs — caused the model to start stripping working features.
rules.audit_note:
Tagged "grounded" with "(none given)" for caveats, but the rule's own source material contradicts that confidence. The exploration doc's Challenge notes for exactly this direction (the RECAP/OGR + Ruff-RL-reward evidence) state it explicitly: "generalised from narrow automated patch-refinement pipelines; the winning result covers one of four tested configurations," with an unexecuted falsification test for whether the gate still pays outside SWE-bench bug-fixing (agentic refactoring, long-horizon tasks). More broadly, the doc's own verdict on all fifteen directions drawn from this corpus is "All fifteen came back weakened. None survived... evidence drawn from a setting that does not transfer... and a statement scoped wider than the finding under it" — and this rule is exactly that pattern: the evidence is patch-refinement/bug-fix-specific (RECAP on SWE-bench agents, an RL training loop with a Ruff reward on two small code-gen models, one Reddit anecdote), but the rule text governs "a change" unqualified, which — combined with the locked design's own "gate is stated once, universally, inherited by every surface" — extends a single-domain result to all five surfaces and to all change types (not just bug-fix patches). None of the cited claims are [!!]-flagged or blocklisted, and the direction of the claim (subordinate simplicity signal to correctness, never let it gate alone) is real and is exactly what the locked SYMMETRIC GATE decision already settled on — so the rule's substance is sound and should be kept. The defect is purely in the status tag and the missing caveat, not in the instruction itself.

RESOLVED 2026-09-11: the reviewer test's second VIOLATES clause ('accepted on the grounds that it's simpler while the correctness check fails or was never run') restated G1's re-run requirement inside the core, where every line is paid on every firing (assembly.duplication_found item 3). Cut. G1 owns the re-run condition; G3 owns only the question of what may decide.

rules.text: For every surface other than code — specs, agent-facing docs, human-facing docs, and the agent's own conversational output — there is no evidenced check that plays the role the test suite plays for code. State that plainly once, in the gate section that covers every surface, and do not invent a substitute gate (a doc linter, a length cap, a self-rated clarity or simplicity score) to stand in for one that doesn't exist.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if guidance for a non-code surface proposes or implies a mechanical pass/fail check to gate a simplification there, without naming that no such check exists. SATISFIES if it states the limitation explicitly and routes the decision to human judgment instead of a mechanical substitute.
rules.evidence: The exploration document's own consolidation pass states this directly: 'The correctness gate — the single best-validated intervention in the corpus — has no evidenced analogue for documents, specs, or human-facing docs. Three directions state this limit in their own text rather than papering over it.' This is a documented absence, not an inference.
rules.audit_note:
Two issues, both fixable without touching the core claim.

1. Locked-design conflict: "State that plainly wherever this skill governs those surfaces" invites restating the gate's no-analogue caveat in every surface section. Locked.md is explicit that the gate "is stated ONCE, universally, and inherited by every surface. Never restated per surface" — and SKILL.md has a 500-line budget. As written, G4 would push a drafter toward exactly the per-surface repetition the design forbids. Fixed in revised_text by changing the instruction to "state ... once, in the gate section."

2. Reviewer-test loophole: VIOLATES fires only when guidance "proposes or implies a mechanical pass/fail check ... without naming that no such check exists." A draft can satisfy that literal wording while still breaking the rule's substance — e.g. "No evidenced check exists for specs; as a heuristic, keep them under 200 words" names the absence AND invents the length cap the rule text forbids, but the VIOLATES clause as written doesn't catch it because the check only fires on the omission, not on naming-plus-inventing-anyway. The reviewer test should be tightened to fire when a mechanical check is proposed for a non-code surface OR the limitation is omitted — not only the latter. This doesn't change the verdict but should travel with the rule so whoever finalizes REVIEWER TEST text closes the gap.

Evidence check: the CLAIMED EVIDENCE is a verbatim, correctly-quoted line from the exploration doc's consolidation pass (line 340), itself grounded in the locked design's own "Surfaces" section ("The correctness gate has NO evidenced analogue outside code — say so explicitly, offer no substitute"). No [!!]-marked or blocklisted claim is invoked. No magnitude present. The claim is about the state of the corpus itself (an absence), not a result transferred across domains, so the usual transfer risk doesn't apply here. "Grounded" is an honest tag for the core claim; the illustrative examples (doc linter, length cap, self-rated score) are not themselves evidentiary claims and shouldn't be read as such.

rules.text:
For duplicated code, ask whether the two regions would need to change together to stay correct — not whether the text looks similar. Duplication tied to a shared underlying requirement that forces synchronized edits across both copies is the kind worth flagging. Duplication between regions that are deliberately independent (different callers, different lifecycles, no shared requirement forcing them to move together) is frequently fine on its own and is not automatically a defect.
Falsification: Kapser & Godfrey's good-clone fraction is unstable across their own four samples, so the criterion is better attested than the proportion. If duplicates that would not need to co-evolve cause faults at the same rate as those that would, the question separates nothing and textual similarity was the better signal.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a duplication flag (or a dedup suggestion) is justified only by textual similarity, with no claim about whether the two regions share a requirement that would force synchronized change. SATISFIES if the verdict — flag or leave alone — states whether the two regions are tied to a shared requirement that would force them to co-evolve.
rules.evidence: D1-5: Kapser & Godfrey's classification criteria (§4.2) state the deciding question for likely-harmful clones is whether the copies are likely to require synchronized co-evolution — this is the literal criterion, not a paraphrase. Their 2008 EMSE paper's headline 'as many as 71% good clones' figure is the best of four case-study samples; the full range across systems and thresholds is 71%/42%/33%/57%, not a stable estimate. Corroborated by Juergens et al. (roughly half of clone groups inconsistent, about half of those a confirmed fault) as the harmful baseline this test is meant to separate out.
rules.audit_note: The load-bearing citation (Kapser & Godfrey §4.2's co-evolution criterion, claims.txt line 467) carries no verification mark at all — not [OK], not [--] — so "the literal criterion, not a paraphrase" is the author's own reading of the source PDF, not something the corpus pass confirmed; tolerable under a precautionary tag but not free. Separately, the reviewer test only checks that a co-evolution claim was stated ("these are independent callers"), not that it's true — it gates the form of the justification, not its correctness, which an agent could satisfy with unverified boilerplate.

rules.text: Before keeping or cutting a standing rule (a CLAUDE.md entry, a skill instruction, a prompt line), do not decide by imagining what would happen without it — that is the same unaided prediction this skill distrusts everywhere else. Remove the rule, run the task(s) it exists to protect, and observe whether the mistake it targets actually occurs. Keep the rule only if the mistake reappears without it; cut it if the task still goes fine without it.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a rule's keep/cut decision is defended only by a predicted counterfactual ('without this the agent would probably…'), with no run recorded. SATISFIES if the decision cites an actual removal-and-rerun — even one informal before/after pair — and states the observed outcome.
rules.evidence: D3-harness-practice: Claude Code's own documented pruning test is 'would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?' — grounded as a real, cited practice, but stated and applied there as a predicted judgment, not an executed one. The exploration document's direction 4 ('execute the removal test, don't ask an LLM to predict it') is the locked design's basis for converting the predicted form into an executed one.
rules.audit_note: Minor, non-blocking notes for the orchestrator rather than defects in the rule text itself. (1) The rule's underlying decision criterion ("cut if the task goes fine without it") is actually grounded, not just judgment: claims.txt:307 has Claude Code's own docs saying "If Claude already does something correctly without the instruction, delete it." Only the *executed-not-predicted* method is invented/judgment — worth noting in the write-up so "judgment" is understood as covering the execution mechanism, not the underlying keep/cut question. (2) Per locked.md, a falsification one-liner must ship inline with every rule, and this packet's TEXT field contains none — can't tell if it lives elsewhere. If/when it's added, it must NOT carry the exploration doc's "3-5 runs per arm" figure (line 300 of the exploration doc), since that is a magnitude and locked design bars magnitudes; a compliant version would read something like "run the removal test twice on the same rule — if the two verdicts disagree, treat the test as noise, not signal." (3) The reviewer test's allowance of "even one informal before/after pair" is a count but functions as an evidentiary floor (predicted vs. executed), not an effect-size claim like the blocklisted percentages — I judge it exempt from NO MAGNITUDES, but flag the ruling explicitly since a later adversarial pass may contest it.

rules.text: Outside these two tests, there is no review-time check for over-engineering. The only clean definition the corpus converges on is retrospective — complexity counts as over-engineering only if it anticipated a requirement that never materialized, and identical code is good engineering if the requirement arrives. For every other surface (complexity in code generally, specs, agent-facing docs, human-facing docs, conversational output), name what looks speculative or unused and say why, but treat that as a flagged judgment call to raise for a human, not a pass/fail check this skill can adjudicate.
rules.reviewer_test: diagnosis only — no reviewer test
rules.evidence: Exploration document, Theme 'detection is the weakest link' (line 78) and Framing section (line 17): 'Over-engineering has no review-time definition... Every review-time test in this document is a proxy for a fact that has not happened yet.' This is the document's own stated headline finding, drawn from an independently-observed practitioner consensus (facet E1) that the corpus's research process treated as first-class evidence requiring independent cross-thread confirmation.

rules.text:
Never ship or cite a cyclomatic-complexity band, a method or function line-count cap, a dead-code percentage, or a cohesion score (LCOM and kin) as the reason for a simplicity or complexity verdict — in a review comment, a lint rule, or an agent's own justification. Argue the verdict through the co-evolution question or an executed removal test, or leave it as a named, unadjudicated judgment call.
Falsification: the ban rests on misattribution — the specific thresholds people cite do not trace to the sources invoked for them. If one of these metrics is validated against defect or maintenance outcomes on an independent corpus, the ban on that metric lapses; the others stand on their own failures.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a complexity or simplicity verdict cites a cyclomatic-complexity band, a line-count cap, a dead-code percentage, or an LCOM/cohesion score as its reason. SATISFIES if the same verdict is instead argued through the co-evolution question, an executed removal test, or is left as a named, unadjudicated judgment call.
rules.evidence:
Claims.txt: cyclomatic-complexity thresholds as an over-engineering detector [!!]-failed; dead-code prevalence percentages [!!]-failed; Lack-of-Cohesion-in-Methods (LCOM) as a detector [!!]-failed. These three are misattribution failures: the claims cited for these thresholds do not trace to the sources invoked for them, which is by itself sufficient reason never to cite them as a review comment's justification. The underlying verification facts for the McCabe and dead-code entries are recorded once in M1's blocklist and are not restated here.

Method and function line-count limits have no matching [!!] detector-claim, so they rest on different evidence: the exploration doc's depth-round finding that the 24-line-method study's own maintenance-effort direction reverses when the same dataset is expressed as defect/change density rather than raw totals — the paper's own summary says the direction depends on which dependent variable is chosen. That rules out a clean line-count cutoff on its own.
rules.audit_note:
The rule's core prohibition is sound and directly mandated by locked.md, but its CLAIMED EVIDENCE overreaches in two ways checkable in the corpus. First, it cites Shepperd's "CC is largely a proxy for LOC" critique and Landman et al.'s weak-correlation finding side by side as if they "corroborate" the same caution — but they are opposing answers to the same question, and the exploration doc says so explicitly ("the popular cyclomatic-complexity-is-just-SLOC critique is itself overstated... the debunk needs debunking," line 68). Landman's finding argues CC is NOT redundant with LOC, which is the opposite of what the rule's gloss ("too weak... to support... a clean threshold") implies; that phrase is an inference the source doesn't make — a genuine overread. Second, "a method or function line-count limit" is one of four banned items in TEXT but has zero citation in CLAIMED EVIDENCE: no [!!]-tagged claim in claims.txt targets line-count limits as a detector (the only [!!] items are CC-threshold, dead-code%, and LCOM). Real support for banning line-count limits exists — the exploration doc's line-329 finding that the 24-line-method study's direction reverses under a density measure — but the rule never cites it, leaving one of its four prohibitions evidentially unsupported as written even though the locked design independently mandates it.

RESOLVED 2026-09-11: the Shepperd/Landman pairing the audit flagged as an overread is dropped rather than reworded — it is not needed once the [!!] misattributions carry the CC-threshold prohibition on their own, and Landman's finding argues CC is not redundant with LOC, the opposite of what the old gloss implied. The D1-6 architectural-decay finding is also dropped from this rule: it is genuine and separately verified but concerns a metric outside the four banned categories, so citing it here was gesturing at corroboration rather than supplying it. Author's caveat, carried forward: the line-count ban and the CC/dead-code/LCOM ban rest on different evidence types — an unreplicated reversal finding versus misattribution — and are treated as equally sufficient because locked.md mandates this exact list, not because they carry equal evidentiary weight.

Also resolved 2026-09-11: this rule's text field had held the auditor's editing memo ("TEXT and REVIEWER TEST: keep as written...", "CLAIMED EVIDENCE — replace with:") rather than any rule text. The rule above was written from the memo's instructions and the surviving reviewer test; the memo's replacement evidence paragraph now occupies the evidence field as the memo directed.

rules.text:
Judge these signals at the level of the diff or the change as a whole, never a single function in isolation. A function can look lean and short while the surrounding change adds files, layers, or options that add up to over-production — function-level simplicity and diff-level simplicity are different measurements, and the corpus that finds AI-written functions simpler than human ones is not the same corpus that finds AI-written systems accumulating duplication and scope creep.
Falsification: this rests on two corpora disagreeing by unit of analysis — AI-written functions measure leaner, AI-written systems accumulate. If a single corpus finds both at the same level of analysis, the distinction this rule draws collapses.
rules.reviewer_test: diagnosis only — no reviewer test. This governs how S2–S6 are applied to a draft, not a checkable property of the draft itself.
rules.evidence: C2-ai-code-complexity's 500k-function comparison finds AI-generated functions shorter and structurally simpler than human ones, while C3-agent-failure-modes' project-level studies (and the D2-2 real-repo diff-in-diff results) find AI-generated systems accumulate duplication, scope creep, and unrequested dependencies. The exploration doc names this directly: 'whether AI over-engineers depends entirely on the unit of analysis.' D1-1 frames the same tension and leaves it unresolved rather than adjudicated.
rules.audit_note:
The rule's first clause (judge at diff/change level, not isolated function level) is fairly supported by the exploration doc's "unit of analysis" theme: C2's 507k-function study finds AI functions shorter/simpler while C3's project-level studies and D2-2's real-repo diff-in-diff studies find AI systems decaying — a genuine, cited measurement split, exactly as the author's evidence section describes. That much earns "precautionary."

But the second clause — "the reverse practically never happens" — is unsupported invention. Nothing in claims.txt measures or bounds how often a function looks complex while its enclosing diff stays lean; no claim addresses that direction at all. Worse, it sits in tension with evidence that IS in the corpus: D1-1 records that "In C3's own function-level experiment (Experiment I, CodeContest algorithmic problems vs. a verified human solution), more capable models produced MORE method bloat than the human baseline, not less — the opposite direction addressed in the 507k study." That is a documented case of complexity showing up at the function level itself, which undercuts confidence in a blanket "practically never" claim about the reverse pattern. This is the exact failure the audit is watching for: an inference (near-total asymmetry) that goes well beyond, and is arguably contradicted by, its own source material. The author's caveat concedes the tension "dissolves rather than resolving" and is "not a mechanism" — that caveat applies to the whole framing, but the asymmetry assertion is the part that most overclaims, since even the documented split doesn't establish directionality this strongly. Cutting that clause leaves an honest, evidence-backed scoping instruction; keeping it lets an untested frequency claim ride along as if it had the same evidentiary weight as the studies actually cited.

No magnitude/blocklist violation, no [!!] evidence, and the diagnosis-only status (no reviewer VIOLATES/SATISFIES test) is an acceptable honest answer per the locked hard-constraint exception for scoping instructions — that part need not change.

rules.text:
A new config flag, environment variable, settings option, or dependency introduced without the task calling for configurability or the added package is a signal, not a default good practice.
Falsification: the finding is observational — agents introduce unrequested dependencies and configuration — and was never measured against whether the added configurability was later used. If unrequested config is exercised as often as requested config, this is a preference and not a signal.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a new configurable parameter or dependency is set once, in one place, and nothing in the task asks for it to vary or be added. SATISFIES if the task, an existing convention, or a named future caller calls for it.
rules.evidence: C3-agent-failure-modes: 'Unnecessary dependencies: agents introduce unnecessary functionalities, unwanted dependencies, and unrequested architectural choices' (peer). Devin case study: 'configuration layers for imaginary scale' (prac). Corroborating but tangential: C3's missing-dependency-declaration and dependency-multiplier findings, which show agents mismanage the dependency surface in both directions.
rules.audit_note: Minor, non-fatal: the rule's enumerated vocabulary ("config flag, environment variable, settings option") is a generalization from the cited evidence's actual wording ("unwanted dependencies, and unrequested architectural choices" / "configuration layers"), not a verbatim match — a fair but inferential extension, not a reversal. The "environment variable" and "settings option" items specifically aren't named in either source; they're read into "architectural choices" / "configuration layers." This is within normal interpretive latitude, not overreach severe enough to cut or revise.

rules.text:
When editing a CLAUDE.md, skill file, or AGENTS.md, convert descriptive or narrative passages (background, philosophy, repository overviews) into concrete directives, or delete them — independent of what that does to the resulting length.
Falsification: the repo-context study found descriptive overviews unhelpful while concrete instructions were followed. If descriptive context measurably improves task success in a test that controls for length, the convert-or-delete direction is wrong.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if an edit to an agent-facing doc trims length or reorders sections but leaves descriptive/overview prose intact; SATISFIES if it converts or removes descriptive prose in favor of checkable directives, regardless of resulting line count.
rules.evidence: B1-agent-docs / D1-3: 'A rigorous evaluation of repository-level context files ... found providing such files does not generally improve task success ... concrete instructions were well followed; descriptive repository overviews ... were not helpful' (arXiv 2602.11988). Direction 11 in the exploration doc names this the surviving text-shaped lever.

rules.text:
When a diff adds a rule to an agent-facing doc, check the resulting doc for an existing rule that already covers substantially the same ground. Merge or cut the overlap rather than leaving both standing.
Falsification: the three benchmarks behind this measure independent simultaneous constraints, not overlapping ones. If merging two overlapping rules does not improve compliance over leaving both standing, the transfer from constraint count to rule overlap does not hold.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a diff adds a rule to an agent-facing doc and the result leaves two live rules covering substantially the same ground, with neither merged nor cut. SATISFIES if no such overlap exists in the result, or an overlapping existing rule was merged or cut as part of the same change.
rules.evidence: B1-agent-docs: FollowBench Hard Satisfaction Rate falls 84.7%→61.9% (GPT-4) at 5 vs. 1 constraints; IFScale — even the best of 20 frontier models hits only 68% accuracy at maximum instruction density; ComplexBench — GPT-4 collapses to 14.9% under its stricter composition scoring. All three converge on the same shape: compliance falls monotonically as simultaneous constraints accumulate.
rules.audit_note:
Two defects, both fixable by re-anchoring the rule to a post-hoc diagnostic instead of a precondition on adding.

(1) Locked-decision conflict. locked.md states plainly, under Claims: "Rule admission is ungoverned (the incident-required gate was considered and dropped)." The parenthetical explains *why* (one candidate gate — trace-to-incident, exploration direction 8 — was weighed and rejected as self-implicating in the exploration doc's own tension analysis), but the locked principle itself is unqualified: no precondition gates whether a rule may be added. D2 as authored imposes exactly such a precondition — its REVIEWER TEST makes VIOLATES turn on whether "a corresponding removal, merge, or consolidation" was considered *before* the addition is allowed to stand clean. That is a precondition on admission, structurally the same move as the rejected incident-gate even though its substance (search-for-overlap vs. trace-to-incident) differs. Per the audit brief, a rule conflicting with a locked decision is wrong regardless of merit. The fix is to move the check from before-the-add (a gate) to after-the-diff (a diagnostic on the resulting state) — symmetric with how the already-shipped co-evolution and pruning tests are applied afterward, not as entry conditions.

(2) The second sentence ("treat the count of simultaneously live rules as a budget to manage, not a total that only grows") is pure exhortation — it adds no independently checkable condition beyond the first sentence and the reviewer test doesn't cite it. Cut for concision; the rule set has a tight line budget and this bought nothing operative.

Evidence and status hold up on their own: the FollowBench/IFScale/ComplexBench quotes are verified verbatim against claims.txt (all [OK], none blocklisted), the rule text carries no magnitude, and `precautionary` is the right tag — three converging general instruction-following benchmarks extended by inference to a persistent coding-agent doc, exactly the shape the scannable-prose skill's own A4/B1/B3/C4 precedent tags `precautionary`. The author's caveat about D2-1's confound (file size varied, not rule count independently) is honest and doesn't need to move the status — that study isn't cited as support, only disclosed as an unresolved counter-signal.

rules.text: Keep tool descriptions short — every token in a tool description is paid by every candidate-tool comparison. Cut a sentence only if removing it would not change whether the tool gets selected or how the call gets filled in (marketing framing, implementation rationale, restated context are the usual offenders).
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a tool description carries a sentence that would not change whether an agent picks the tool or how it fills in the call (marketing framing, implementation rationale, restated context); SATISFIES if every sentence bears on the selection or invocation decision.
rules.evidence: B1-agent-docs, [OK] verified: tool descriptions carry a measurable token tax — at roughly 200 tokens each, a shortlist of 100 candidate tools consumes about 20,000 tokens before the actual query is processed. [OK] verified: function-calling accuracy degrades sharply as tool catalogs or their descriptive context grow, even within a stated large context window.
rules.audit_note: The two [OK]-verified claims (200-token/description tax scaling to ~20K tokens across a 100-tool shortlist; function-calling accuracy dropping 7.59-85.58% as tool catalogs/context grow) are both volume claims: more tools, more total tokens, worse selection accuracy. Neither claim manipulates or measures *which kind of content within one description* matters — they say nothing about rationale vs. purpose/parameters/constraints as a meaningful split. D4's prescription (differentiate "selection-relevant" content from "rationale/background/philosophy" and cut only the latter) is machinery invented on top of a coarser, real finding, exactly the "statement scoped wider than the finding under it" pattern the exploration doc's challenge pass flagged in 15/15 directions (e.g. direction 11's density-lever overreach, direction 3's scope-widening). The evidence licenses "make tool descriptions shorter / catalogs smaller"; it does not license "the correct way to shorten is by category of content." Tagging this grounded overstates what B1-agent-docs actually shows. The claim does transfer well (it's drawn from live tool-calling/function-calling studies, not chat/QA benchmarks like most of the corpus), and neither cited line is [!!] or blocklisted, so this is not a cut — it's a status correction plus a text tightened to the coarser, actually-supported claim while preserving the same reviewer test.

rules.text:
If a rule in a static agent-facing doc keeps getting missed only deep into a session (not near the start), editing that passage in place — lengthening it, re-emphasizing it, restating it — is unlikely to be the fix: the one controlled test of CLAUDE.md structure found that file-shaped variables (length, position, architecture, a conflicting rule) move where compliance starts, not how it decays within a session, and generation volume was the only thing that did. No out-of-band countermeasure — hooks, re-dispatch, or anything else — has been run as a controlled intervention on a coding agent, so this is a name for a failure mode, not a validated fix. Treat repeated deep-session misses as a signal to look for a mechanism outside the static file, not as license to assume any particular one (including re-stating the rule at a subagent dispatch) will work.
Falsification: the diagnosed pattern is that deep-session misses are not fixed by editing the passage. If a controlled test shows in-place edits do recover deep-session compliance, this is wrong — and the single study behind it is a single-author preprint on a single-turn harness with a grep-detectable marker instruction.
rules.reviewer_test: diagnosis-not-enforcement — no reviewer test. A reviewer can recognize the pattern (repeated misses land deep into a session, not at the start) but the corpus licenses no specific remedy to check compliance against, so no VIOLATES/SATISFIES verdict is claimed.
rules.evidence: D2-1: 'the single largest measured effect on instruction compliance was within-session: each additional function the coding agent generated' predicted non-compliance, while none of the file-structure variables (size, position, architecture, a conflicting rule) did. Matches the locked design claim: guidance shifts the starting point and does not change the degradation rate.
rules.audit_note:
Two distinct overreaches, both in the prescriptive half of the rule (the diagnosis half is defensible):

1. Invented, unevidenced mechanism. D2-1's evidence supports only the diagnosis: text-shaped file variables (length, position, architecture, a conflicting rule) don't move the within-session decay rate; generation volume does. It says nothing about "dispatch points" or "a subagent's prompt" as a remedy. The source paper's own top recommendation for counteracting drift is hooks (PreToolUse/PostToolUse) — and the exploration doc is explicit that even *that* recommendation "has never been run as a controlled intervention on a coding agent" (explorations doc line 321, "Hook-based mid-session re-injection is untested") and that "No drift mechanism is validated on a coding agent" (line 339). D5's prescribed fix (subagent-prompt re-assertion) is a different, even-less-evidenced mechanism than the one the source paper itself floats untested. Grep of claims.txt confirms zero claims mention subagent prompts, dispatch points, or re-assertion at dispatch as a tested intervention. This is exactly the overreach pattern the exploration doc's own Challenge note warns against: "a design must name which drift hypothesis it is betting on rather than presenting re-injection as settled" (line 176) — D5 presents its bet as settled ("Re-assert the constraint at the next dispatch point instead," stated as a flat instruction, not a hedge).

2. Self-contradictory reviewer test. The REVIEWER TEST is written as a binary, mandate-style VIOLATES/SATISFIES verdict on real drafts ("VIOLATES if... SATISFIES if...") — full enforcement. But the same field then appends "Diagnosis-not-enforcement for the general claim itself — no drift-correction mechanism is evidenced enough to mandate." Those two clauses cannot both be true: a test that assigns VIOLATES/SATISFIES to a specific fix choice *is* mandating that fix. The rule wants credit for being both an enforceable check and an honest non-mandate at once.

The locked design's carve-out ("explicitly labelled diagnosis-not-enforcement") is the right shape for what the evidence actually supports here — but D5 needs to actually take that shape (no binary verdict tied to a specific unevidenced remedy), not gesture at it while keeping the mandate. Separately: locked.md's "anyone dispatching a subagent must restate the gate in the subagent's prompt" is a governance rule specific to the Part-2 correctness gate; D5 leans on that precedent to make its invented general drift-remedy sound familiar, but the gate-restatement rule is a locked architectural decision, not evidence that dispatch-point restatement fixes arbitrary rule-drift.

rules.text:
Flag any provision in a spec — a requirement, field, config knob, or extensibility point the document commits to build or support — whose only stated justification is an anticipated future need ("so we can later...", "in case...", "for extensibility") and that names no consumer, ticket, or test presently in scope. This does not apply to a Non-goals section or a stated exclusion, which by design names nothing, nor to an ordinary requirement that simply doesn't cite a consumer inline. Spec length is not itself a signal either way: a long spec whose every provision serves a present need or traces to a present consumer satisfies this test, and a short one with a single speculatively-justified, untraceable provision does not.
Falsification: the length-is-not-the-signal half is convergent across four independent spec standards; the speculative-provision half is the exploration's own retrospective framing. If provisions justified only by anticipated need are exercised as often as provisions naming a present consumer, the flag has no predictive content.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a provision is justified only by anticipated future need ('so we can later...', 'in case...', 'for extensibility') with no consumer, ticket, or test named in current scope — regardless of how long or short the surrounding document is. SATISFIES if every provision traces to something presently named, or the document contains no such provisions.
rules.evidence: Direction 12 / facet B2-spec-bloat, built on the exploration's own headline synthesis that over-engineering is only decidable in retrospect. The length-is-not-the-signal clause is convergent across three independent standards in B2: Nygard's original ADR template specifies one to two pages, Google's design-doc guidance runs an order of magnitude longer for larger projects, and the Rust RFC process and IETF RFC 2360 both explicitly decline to set length rules, holding that consensus and clarity matter more than size.
rules.audit_note:
Two distinct issues, one structural (the real defect), one evidentiary (secondary).

(1) TEXT and REVIEWER TEST don't match, and TEXT is the overbroad one. TEXT says: flag "any provision... that names no consumer, ticket, or test presently in scope" — full stop. Taken literally, that fires on essentially every ordinary requirement in any real spec, since specs routinely state functionality ("email: string, required," "supports pagination with a default page size") without inline-citing a consumer, ticket, or test — not because it's speculative, but because normal prose doesn't footnote every field. REVIEWER TEST is narrower and sane: VIOLATES only fires when a provision "is justified only by anticipated future need ('so we can later...', 'in case...', 'for extensibility')" AND names nothing current; SATISFIES covers "the document contains no such provisions" (i.e., no anticipatorily-justified ones) even when plenty of ordinary fields cite no consumer at all. So the REVIEWER TEST — which is what a reviewer would actually apply — holds up fine on a real draft. TEXT, read on its own as the shipped rule, does not: it would flag mundane, obviously in-scope requirements as violations, which is exactly the false-positive-explosion failure mode the corpus's own Challenge notes call out repeatedly ("statement scoped wider than the finding under it"), and exactly the kind of unanchored simplicity pressure the exploration's "destroys function" theme warns against if agents start stripping ordinary fields to satisfy the letter of the rule.

(2) Secondary, evidentiary: the CLAIMED EVIDENCE frames the "spec length is not itself a signal" clause as resting on "convergent" support from three B2 standards (Nygard's 1-2 page ADRs, Google's longer design docs, Rust RFC/IETF's refusal to set a length rule). None of those sources address the question the clause actually needs support for — whether spec length correlates with untraceable provisions. They establish that recommended document length varies by document type/purpose, which is a different claim. The length-agnosticism clause is actually just an analytic corollary of the rule's own per-provision construction (once fixed per #1) — it doesn't need evidentiary backing and citing B2 as "convergent" evidence for it overclaims. This doesn't break the rule, but it's a "scoped wider than the finding" pattern the audit should not wave through.

rules.text: A tech spec layered over an approved logic spec earns its place only by committing to at least one choice the logic spec left open — one a reviewer could name as what the implementer would otherwise have had to decide alone. A tech spec whose every commitment is copied from the logic spec, or is its only possible reading, has earned nothing by existing. Diagnosis, not enforcement: this is not independently checkable at review time — a tech spec built to the existing template (code-anchored pointers, contracts, DO-NOT-CHANGE fences) already tends to satisfy it, and a spec that doesn't already fails the writing-specs reviewer's Pointer-precision, Completeness, and Buildability checks.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if no section of the second document narrows a choice the first document left open — everything in it is inferable from the first document plus headers, diagrams, or reformatting. SATISFIES if at least one section commits to a specific mechanism, structure, or path at a point where the first document left the choice open, even without the rejected alternative or rationale appearing inline.
rules.evidence: Direction 12, facet B2-spec-bloat. This repo's own writing-specs rubric already polices the inverse of this rule — 'if a section reads like it belongs in the logic spec — rationale, alternatives, conceptual framing — cut it' (skills/writing-specs/tech-spec.md:57) — and its reviewer prompt checks Fidelity, that every locked decision from the first document is implemented somewhere in the second (skills/writing-specs/tech-spec-reviewer-prompt.md:35), which a pure restatement passes trivially. Neither existing check verifies the second document adds a decision; this rule fills that specific gap.
rules.audit_note: Three compounding problems. (1) Locked-constraint violation: locked.md's DETECTION rule says to ship ONLY the two surviving review-time tests (co-evolution, pruning) and to state explicitly that every other surface "is not checkable at review time" — S2 ships a third enforceable VIOLATES/SATISFIES reviewer test scoped to specs, which the hard-constraints section anticipates only as "cut or explicitly labelled diagnosis-not-enforcement." (2) The evidence doesn't support what's claimed: direction 12 requires the second document's decision to be "made among named alternatives," but S2 explicitly drops alternatives (per tech-spec.md:57, which forbids alternatives/rationale in tech.md). Once dropped, the SATISFIES bar collapses to "the spec names any implementation-level commitment the logic spec didn't" — which any template-compliant tech.md automatically does (code pointers, contracts, fences per tech-spec.md:46-55 are never inferable from a logic spec). The only specs that would VIOLATES already fail the existing reviewer's Pointer-precision/Completeness/Buildability checks (tech-spec-reviewer-prompt.md:34-39). So "neither existing check verifies the second document adds a decision; this rule fills that gap" is false on a realistic draft — there's no daylight between S2's SATISFIES and the status quo. (3) The claimed evidence is not corpus evidence at all — it's an internal argument about a gap in this repo's own rubric, plus the exploration document's own unevidenced generalization from "tech spec over logic spec" (direction 12's literal scope) to "a document layered on an already-approved one" generally, which the author's own caveat admits is ungrounded. The caveat also misattributes dropping "named alternatives" to the locked deletion-rationale-in-code-comments precedence rule, which doesn't reach spec content; the real (and sufficient) justification is tech-spec.md:57.

rules.text:
S1 and S2 flag stated content — a provision naming no consumer, a second document making no decision among named alternatives — which a code surface cannot offer. They are not gates: no test suite runs before or after cutting what they flag, so a VIOLATES is a content judgment, not a verified pass/fail. Neither sees the opposite failure — a spec that under-specifies and ships a defect-inducing gap.
Falsification: the claim is that these flag stated content and are blind to under-specification. If a reviewer using them catches under-specification defects at the same rate as one not using them, the stated blind spot is not real.
rules.reviewer_test: diagnosis only — no reviewer test. State this explicitly alongside S1 and S2 rather than letting a spec edit read as gated the way a code deletion is.
rules.evidence: The exploration document's own framing synthesis: over-engineering 'has no review-time definition... every review-time test in this document is a proxy for a fact that has not happened yet.' The under-specification blind spot draws on the same B2-spec-bloat counter-findings cited in S1/S2 — requirements-investment correlating with project success, and agile's requirements-defect increase relative to waterfall.
rules.audit_note: Two defects, one wording-level and one structural, plus one thing to verify against the rest of the draft. (1) The opening clause — "unusually checkable because the document states its prediction explicitly" — uses "checkable" to mean merely readable, but locked lines 19 and 62 define "checkable" as a reviewer being able to say VIOLATES/SATISFIES, i.e. decidable. In a rule whose entire job is to stop the skill from overclaiming a gate for specs, the opening line uses the design's own load-bearing term in the opposite sense, and the rest of the rule then spends its length walking that claim back. (2) That same opening clause also conflates S1 and S2 under one rationale — "the document states its prediction explicitly" fits S1 (a provisioning claim is an implicit prediction) but not S2 (a restating document's problem is an absent decision, not a stated prediction) — attributing S1's evidentiary basis to a flag it doesn't cover. Neither issue touches the corpus citations themselves, which check out: the "proxy for a fact that has not happened yet" quote is accurate, the two B2-spec-bloat studies (requirements-investment/success correlation, waterfall-vs-agile requirements-defect) are unflagged, not on the blocklist, and are used with appropriate hedging (status stays precautionary, no magnitude asserted). Direction 12's own falsifier — strip flagged unnamed-consumer provisions from real specs and count urgent unplanned retrofits — is in-corpus and more directly on point for the under-specification sentence than the waterfall/agile study (which hedges with "may" and attributes defects to a methodology switch, not to spec thinness); citing it alongside would strengthen that sentence, though its absence isn't disqualifying. (3) Unverified from this rule's text alone: locked line 8 says the gate is stated once, universally, and never restated per surface, and locked line 32 already puts "no evidenced analogue outside code" into that universal statement. If Part 2 already says this, S3's middle sentence duplicates it, and the rule's only non-redundant content is the under-specification blind-spot sentence — check S3 against the actual Part 2 text before shipping.

rules.text: Before adding a new standing document, check for an existing indexed, maintained surface — another doc, a README section, the schema or code itself, or a single ticket/incident record that already holds the full answer — that answers the question in one place. A surface that would force the reader to piece the answer together across multiple tickets or chat threads does not count. If such a surface exists, extend or link it instead of adding a new document; if none does, or the existing surface only holds scattered raw facts rather than the answer itself, the new document is justified.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a draft adds a new document restating content that already exists, answered in one place, in another current indexed doc or page, with no stated reason it couldn't go there instead. SATISFIES if the draft names the surface it checked and the specific gap — including 'the facts exist but only scattered across tickets/threads, not as an answer' as a valid gap.
rules.evidence: Exploration direction 14's creation-side check. Its own falsification test says a document whose raw facts were 'technically already scattered across old tickets and threads' should NOT have been blocked by a naive version of this check — that's why the rule requires the existing surface to answer in one place, not merely contain the facts somewhere. E3-reddit-docs corroborates both directions: 'Confluence is where documentation goes to die' is independently observed across 3+ threads (docs get created and go unused, motivating a real check before creating), while the knowledge-base-vs-Slack-search finding shows relying on chat as a substitute for documentation is itself a reported pathology, not a satisfying alternative.
rules.audit_note: The rule's own exclusion clause contradicts its flagship motivating evidence. TEXT explicitly disqualifies 'tickets' as a way of already answering a question ('not one whose facts a reader would have to assemble by searching across tickets or chat threads'), placing tickets in the same disqualified bucket as scattered chat threads. But CLAIMED EVIDENCE's primary example is the practitioner complaint about leadership mandating a redundant SITREP/AAR despite the same information 'already existing in ServiceNow, Jira, and Confluence' -- i.e., existing tickets. Run that exact motivating scenario through the rule as written: since the answer lives in ticket systems, the rule's own exclusion clause says those tickets don't count as 'answering in one place,' so the new SITREP would be JUSTIFIED under HD1's escape valve, not blocked. The evidence used to justify the rule is a case the rule as drafted would not actually catch. This is a genuine internal-consistency defect, not a fatal evidence overreach: the core insight (check an existing surface before creating a new standing doc) is reasonably supported by the E3-reddit-docs claims (none marked [!!], none blocklisted, correctly tagged 'judgment' not 'grounded'), no magnitude is present, and the discriminator that resolves direction 14's own falsification test (scattered raw facts vs. an assembled answer) is honestly disclosed as invented rather than passed off as evidenced. The fix is narrow: distinguish 'a single consolidated ticket/record that already holds the answer' (should count as a qualifying surface, matching the motivating example) from 'facts scattered across many tickets/threads requiring assembly' (should not count) -- the current wording collapses both into 'tickets' and disqualifies them wholesale.

rules.text: Apply this test to a document that restates content also tracked as the authoritative copy elsewhere (a ticketing or incident system, code, config, another doc): if nothing keeps the two synchronized on update, treat the restatement as unmanaged risk. Default to reducing the document to a pointer/index into the system of record rather than a full parallel copy. Where reducing it to a pointer is impractical, flag it for scheduled owner review instead — a fixed-window staleness flag forcing a human look is the one practice in this corpus actually reported to cut duplication, and it is a lighter, better-attested move than replacing content with a pointer. Delete outright only when the pointer itself would be redundant (the system of record is already easy to find without it), and state that reason explicitly — full deletion is the higher-risk move given this corpus's own finding that deletion of documents correlates with worse retrieval and is the most under-adopted organizing behavior studied.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a document restates content whose system of record is elsewhere, with no update-linking mechanism, and is kept as a full parallel copy with no pointer alternative considered. SATISFIES if the document is the sole source of truth, or has been reduced to a pointer/index rather than a restatement — full deletion without a pointer needs its own stated reason.
rules.evidence: E3-reddit-docs: leadership mandating a full SITREP plus AAR/RCA per incident ticket despite the same information already existing in ServiceNow, Jira, and Confluence generated a large, sympathetic thread against the duplication. E3's one reported practice that actually reduced documentation rot flags documents 'stale' after a fixed window to force an owner review rather than auto-deleting — direction-only support (marked [--]) for review/pointer over blind deletion.
rules.audit_note: The rule's justification chain overreaches in two linked ways. First, its own caveat asserts the co-evolution test is "validated in its home (code) domain" to justify tagging the doc-domain extension as judgment rather than precautionary — but the exploration doc's own Challenge notes for the two directions that used this test (5 and 12) say the opposite: the one causal AI-specific study found a robust null on duplication across three estimators, and the clone typology's own originator (Kapser) concedes the field still doesn't know which clones are harmful. The premise the rule leans on to calibrate its own confidence is itself contested by the corpus, not settled. Second, the rule's prescribed mechanism — replace with a pointer — isn't what the cited E3-reddit-docs evidence actually demonstrates worked. The SITREP/AAR/RCA item is a sympathetic complaint thread (people are annoyed by duplication), not a report that pointer-replacement fixed anything; the corpus's only item explicitly reported as an effective de-rot practice is a different mechanism (flagging documents stale after a fixed window to force owner review), which the rule mentions only as a passing aside rather than as its actual prescription. The rule imports the pointer mechanism by analogy from code (via the contested co-evolution test) rather than from the doc-domain evidence it cites, and states that analogy's grounding more confidently than the corpus supports.

rules.text: A document that carries a contract, SLA, or compliance citation is judged against that obligation, not against traffic, staleness, or overlap with another doc — low or no usage is not evidence the obligation is gone. It may still be merged into a system of record; the obligated content moves with it rather than being cut.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a document carrying a contract, SLA, or compliance citation is flagged for deletion, consolidation, or 'redundant with X' on the basis of usage, staleness, or overlap alone. SATISFIES if such a document is excluded from that pass, with any proposed change to it justified against the obligation instead.
rules.evidence: E3-reddit-docs: a technical writer states customer contracts and SLAs sometimes mandate documentation specificity and completeness, creating a hard floor against compression. B3-doc-systems' only peer-tier documentation-deletion finding (deletion correlates with worse retrieval; deletion is the most under-adopted practice among the knowledge workers studied, both [--]) is directionally consistent with treating deletion as needing a specific stated reason rather than being a default — reinforcing, not establishing, this carve-out.
rules.audit_note:
Two overreaches, both traceable to the source once checked against the corpus.

(1) The blanket exemption "from usage-based pruning entirely — including a check that would otherwise route it to consolidation" is not supported by either cited claim. E3-reddit-docs (a single technical writer, Reddit, "sometimes mandate... creating a hard floor against compression") is about resisting brevity-driven text compression, not about blocking consolidation into an existing system of record. A doc can be merged into a canonical source with its obligated content carried over intact — that satisfies the obligation while still removing genuine duplication, which is exactly the over-production problem this skill exists to catch. As written, the rule lets any doc with a compliance citation attached become permanently un-mergeable regardless of real overlap, which is the harm check 7 asks about: it would entrench the bloat the skill is supposed to reduce. B3-doc-systems (deletion correlates with worse retrieval; deletion is the most under-adopted KM practice, 51 knowledge workers) does not belong in this rule's provenance at all — it's a general personal-document-management finding with no contract/SLA content, and the author's own caveat already concedes the link to this carve-out is the draft's own inference, not a corpus result. The rule should therefore only constrain what happens to the *obligated content* (don't cut it on usage grounds), not forbid consolidation as an operation.

(2) The rule text and its own reviewer test disagree on what's checkable. The rule says "referenced by a contract" (the contract points at the doc — an external fact invisible in a draft); the reviewer test says "carrying a contract... citation" (the doc points at the contract — visible in-draft, and the only framing that clears the locked scoping bar). The revision adopts the reviewer test's framing throughout.

The underlying move — usage/traffic is the wrong yardstick for a document whose purpose is satisfying an external obligation — has no direct empirical backing in the corpus (E3 supports only the narrower "don't compress away specificity" claim); it's sound as domain judgment, not as an evidenced finding, and "judgment" is the correct tag for it — don't let it drift toward "precautionary" on the strength of a single hedged Reddit comment.

rules.text: Don't justify not creating, cutting, or consolidating a document on the grounds that shorter documentation is inherently better — brevity, verbosity, or word count alone is never acceptable grounds. Citing an existing surface that merely "answers the question" — ambient chat history, a wiki page nobody maintains — is not safe grounds either: the closest evidence describes a team that treated ad hoc chat search as sufficient and lost a maintained knowledge base as a result, which is the failure this rule prevents, not a licence for it.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a document-existence recommendation cites length, verbosity, word count, or a general 'could be shorter' preference as its stated justification, or rests on an unmaintained or ad hoc surface without addressing whether that surface's adequacy is itself the failure mode. SATISFIES if the stated justification is neither of those.
rules.evidence: E3-reddit-docs: a technical writer explicitly pushes back on brevity-for-its-own-sake, framing documentation cuts as a symptom of docs being treated as a cost center rather than a quality lever. This reads consistently with B3-doc-systems' only peer-tier finding on the topic — deletion of documents correlates with worse retrieval, and is the least-adopted organizing behavior among the knowledge workers studied — though that finding is quantitatively unverified ([--]).
rules.audit_note:
The rule bundles two very different pieces of content under one evidence citation. (1) "Don't cite brevity alone" and "contract/SLA overrides" are loosely supported by E3-reddit-docs (a single, non-corroborated practitioner voice — the author's own caveat says as much). (2) "An existing surface already answers the question" as affirmative, SATISFIES-level grounds to not-create/cut a document is NOT supported by the CLAIMED EVIDENCE at all (neither E3 nor B3 says this) — it's silently imported from Direction 14 in the exploration doc ("check lifecycle... against a searchable surface"), and the exploration's own Challenge notes (2026-09-10-simplicity.md line ~310) say explicitly about that exact mechanism: "its strongest evidence cuts against its own prescription. The knowledge-base-versus-Slack-search finding is reported in the corpus as a pathology, not as proof that ambient chat history is a satisfying surface that should block a new document," and its falsification test warns that in "the common case" this check "would have blocked a document that deserved to exist." So the rule's SATISFIES branch for ground 1 would mechanically bless the exact scenario the corpus documents as a failure. Additionally the B3 deletion-correlates-with-worse-retrieval finding is [--] (unverified, not [!!] — not an automatic-cut blocklist hit) and is about individual knowledge workers' personal document-deletion habits, a transfer stretch to team/software documentation decisions the rule doesn't acknowledge. No magnitudes present; status tag "judgment" is already honest and should stay.

RESOLVED 2026-09-11: the duplication this rule set's own co-evolution test found here (assembly.duplication_found item 1 — HD4 restating HD2's default-to-pointer ground and HD3's obligation override) is removed by cutting both clauses from HD4's text and its reviewer test. HD4 now carries only its two unique prohibitions; HD2 and HD3 own the system-of-record and obligation logic outright, and a change to either no longer forces a lockstep edit here.

rules.text: Cut a redundant unprompted hedge that restates a point the reply already hedges elsewhere; keep only the instance whose removal would visibly change what the reader does next. A caveat about a genuinely separate risk is not a duplicate and is not touched by this cut.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES: the same point is hedged more than once in one reply, or a surviving hedge could be deleted with no change to what the reader does next. SATISFIES: no point is hedged twice, and deleting any surviving hedge would visibly change the reader's next action.
rules.evidence: Exploration document, direction 15's machinery (the hedge budget), drawn from the same C1-llm-verbosity mechanism as P1B-1 — models under brevity pressure still generate compressible padding, and stacked hedging is a known instance of that padding.
rules.audit_note: Two defects, both fixable without cutting the core idea. (1) Magnitude: "at most one ... per reply" is an invented numeric cap the locked design bans ("NO MAGNITUDES ... direction only, never numbers"), and the author's own caveat admits it — "no experiment in the corpus measures hedge count against reader outcomes to justify that specific threshold over any other." (2) The rule is internally inconsistent about scope: sentence one caps the whole reply to one caveat globally ("at most one ... per reply"), sentence two frames the cut as per-point ("a second hedge on the same point"), and the reviewer test's VIOLATES clause takes the global reading ("two or more ... in one reply"). Under that global reading, a reply with two genuinely independent, both individually load-bearing caveats (e.g., one about rate limits, one about timezone assumptions — each of which would change the reader's next action if deleted) is forced to cut one anyway, directly contradicting the rule's own SATISFIES justification and destroying information the reader needs. That is exactly the check-7 harm: simplicity pressure applied without an anchor to whether the content is actually load-bearing. Separately, the CLAIMED EVIDENCE leans on "correlating with model uncertainty" — but the exploration doc's own challenge note for direction 15 says the cited chat literature "mostly establishes that length is *rewarded*, which is a different claim from length *signalling the model's own uncertainty*," and flags the direction for leaning on the thinner, less-attested story. The corpus entry itself is tagged [--] (unverified), not [OK]. None of this is blocklisted or [!!], so it isn't an automatic cut, and the author already tagged the rule "judgment" rather than overclaiming — that part is honest and should stay.

rules.text:
This skill shifts the agent's starting verbosity and complexity downward. It does not change how fast quality erodes across a long session — expect drift to resume, and don't rely on this skill alone for anything long-running: budget for a fresh review pass, since no countermeasure here is validated against that drift.
Falsification: one [--]-tagged benchmark (SlopCodeBench) found guidance cuts starting verbosity and structural erosion while leaving the degradation rate unchanged. If a replication shows quality guidance also flattens the degradation slope, this honest claim understates what the skill does and should be strengthened.
rules.reviewer_test: diagnosis only — no reviewer test. This is a claim about what the skill itself can promise, not a property checkable on a single draft.
rules.evidence: claims.txt:551 [--] SlopCodeBench (36 problems, 196 checkpoints, 15 agents): explicit quality guidance cuts starting verbosity and structural erosion but leaves the rate of subsequent degradation unchanged. Consistent with exploration lines 19, 130, 176.
rules.audit_note:
The core claim (starting-point shift, unchanged decay rate) is faithfully drawn from claims.txt:551 (SlopCodeBench, 36 problems/196 checkpoints/15 agents, marker [--] = cited-but-not-adversarially-verified, not [!!] and not blocklisted) and matches exploration doc lines 19/130 closely — "structural erosion" is glossed as "complexity," a defensible paraphrase given Hickey's braided/entangled definition of complexity used throughout the doc. That part earns "precautionary" honestly: single-author preprint, unverified marker, and the author's caveat correctly surfaces the line-284 tension against a conflicting (also unvalidated) near-perfect-adherence result. Status tag and diagnosis-only framing are both appropriate and match the locked exception for non-checkable rules. No magnitude appears in the rule text — the locked "direction only" constraint is respected even though the source uses "by up to a third."

The problem is the closing clause: "still plan on re-injection or a fresh review pass." The rule's own CLAIMED EVIDENCE cites exploration line 176 as consistent support, but line 176 itself says: "The corpus's recommended countermeasure is out-of-band re-injection — but a design must name which drift hypothesis it is betting on rather than presenting re-injection as settled." M4 does exactly what its own cited source warns against: it recommends re-injection as a thing to "plan on" without naming a drift hypothesis, i.e. it treats an unvalidated countermeasure as settled practice. The AUTHOR'S OWN CAVEAT block discloses the line-284 tension but is silent on this line-176 caveat despite line 176 being one of the three lines the claim cites as consistent — that's a selective-disclosure gap: the supportive half of a cited source line is kept, the caveat embedded in that same line is dropped.

rules.text: Prose-level mechanics — sentence length, headings, scannability, tightening — belong to writing-scannable-prose, not this skill. This skill is written for Claude Code; running it inside a different harness is a stated assumption, not something it enforces.
