rules.evidence: Locked decision (locked.md Disclosure section: 'Written for Claude Code; state that assumption at the top') combined with the design choice to keep prose mechanics out of this skill's scope.

rules.text: A dispatched subagent starts with a fresh context — it does not inherit this skill's rules. Anyone who hands a subagent the job of applying a fix must restate the correctness gate directly in that subagent's prompt; naming or linking this skill is not enough.
rules.reviewer_test: Read the subagent's dispatch prompt: does it restate the correctness-gate check inline, or only reference this skill by name? A bare reference VIOLATES; the restated gate SATISFIES.
rules.evidence: Locked decision (locked.md Disclosure section, explicit design decision).
rules.audit_note: M6's core mandate ("restate the gate in a dispatched subagent's prompt") is directly supported — locked.md's Disclosure section says exactly that: "Anyone dispatching a subagent must restate the gate in the subagent's prompt." But the rule as drafted overreads that one-liner into "restate the gate's two tests," and that phrase conflates two separate, deliberately-distinguished pieces of the locked design. Per the Shape section, this skill has TWO SEQUENCED JOBS: Part 1 (spot over-production) uses "the two tests that survived adversarial scrutiny" — the co-evolution question and the executed pruning test (see DETECTION). Part 2 ("the gate") is a distinct, later-stage correctness check applied to a fix, described in Content rules as symmetric ("additions AND deletions both pass a correctness check applied afterward") — a single check, not two tests. Locked.md's own "always-on core" phrase even lists them separately: "the gate + the two surviving tests" (three things, not two). So M6's possessive "the gate's two tests" asserts a decomposition of the gate that locked.md never states and structurally contradicts — it silently merges Part 1's detection tests into Part 2's gate. This is exactly the kind of source-overreading check #1 asks about: the general instruction (restate the gate) is grounded, but the specific elaboration (what the gate consists of) is invented and wrong. A reviewer applying the rule's own test literally — "does it restate the gate's two tests inline" — would be checking for the wrong artifact: either missing the correctness gate entirely while restating the two detection tests, or vice versa, since a subagent asked to implement an already-identified fix plausibly only needs Part 2 (the correctness gate), not the Part 1 detection tests used to find the fix in the first place. The unqualified claim that "a dispatched subagent does not inherit this skill's context" is a reasonable, uncontested operational fact about the harness and doesn't need corpus backing, so it isn't itself the problem — the problem is confined to the "two tests" attribution.

rules.text:
A new function, class, interface, or parameter whose only callers anywhere in the codebase — in the diff or outside it — are its own tests is a signal of speculative generality.
Falsification: no falsifying test in the corpus — this tell was reinstated because the corpus names the signal, not because a result measured it. If elements whose only callers are their own tests acquire real callers at the same rate as any other new element, the tell is noise.
rules.why:
S2 violates a locked design decision and must be cut on that basis, independent of its evidentiary merit.

Locked decision (Content rules → DETECTION): "ship ONLY the two tests that survived adversarial scrutiny — (a) the co-evolution question for duplication... (b) the pruning test for rules... State plainly that the other surfaces are not checkable at review time." This is an explicit closed list of exactly two detection heuristics for the surface-code job of spotting over-production. S2 is a third detection heuristic (an orphan-caller/test-only-user tell for speculative generality) that the locked decisions never enumerate and implicitly exclude by saying "ONLY." It is also a close cousin of the explicitly named exclusion "dead-code rates" — S2's tell (only callers are the symbol's own tests) is a boolean variant of unused/dead-code detection, the exact facet the locked doc says failed verification and should not ship.

Tracing the provenance confirms why it was left out rather than merely overlooked: the exploration doc's "two operational tests survived scrutiny" line (line 79) names only co-evolution and the pruning test — matching locked.md's two exactly. The speculative-generality "one mechanical tell" claim sits one line below (line 80) in the Findings synthesis, but it was never one of the 15 directions put through the Challenge gauntlet (co-evolution appears as Direction 5, the pruning test as Direction 4; there is no speculative-generality direction in the 15). So the architects who wrote locked.md had this claim in front of them and chose not to promote it into the "ship" list — plausibly because, per the author's own caveat, it carries no adversarial-verification marker (no [OK] in claims.txt for A3-detection lines 54–55), unlike the two that made the cut.

On the merits the rule is otherwise one of the more defensible candidates in this batch: claim 54 ("(book) ... only users of a function or class are test cases") is read faithfully, not reversed or overreached; it doesn't touch [!!] or blocklisted items; it carries no magnitude; and the reviewer test is genuinely executable (grep for callers, check if only the test file shows up) rather than requiring judgment. But "ship ONLY the two tests" is a hard scope boundary the task instructions say overrides merit — a third, however clean, is not authorized for this skill draft.
rules.reinstated_because: Corpus names a concrete signal; adjudicated 2026-09-11 after the tests-vs-tells distinction was drawn.
rules.reviewer_test: Grep for callers of the new element across the codebase. VIOLATES if the only callers are its own tests. SATISFIES if a non-test caller exists, or the diff names the caller it is being added for.

rules.text:
Before accepting a new helper, utility, or file, check whether the codebase already has one that does this, or already has a convention for solving this problem, before writing a new one. Reaching for a new file or a new pattern that duplicates or diverges from what's already there is a signal.
Falsification: no falsifying test in the corpus — this tell was reinstated because the corpus names the signal, not because a result measured it. The cited findings concern agents ignoring existing codebase context generally, not the narrower failure to reuse an existing helper; if the two come apart, this tell does not follow from them.
rules.why: Two independent problems, either sufficient alone. (1) Locked-decision conflict: the locked design restricts shippable duplication detection to exactly one operational test, stated once and universally — Kapser & Godfrey's co-evolution question ('DETECTION: ship ONLY the two tests that survived adversarial scrutiny ... state plainly the other surfaces are not checkable at review time'). The exploration doc's Direction 5 is explicit that this test survived 'as operational rather than aesthetic' — implying naive existing-equivalent-search checks were the aesthetic alternative that did NOT survive. S6's reviewer test ('an equivalent function, module, or established local pattern already exists and the diff didn't reuse it') is exactly that rejected naive duplication check, reintroduced under a 'surface-code' label instead of the sanctioned co-evolution question. Shipping it would be a second, competing detection instrument for the same underlying problem (duplication) that the locked decisions forbid — wrong regardless of merit. (2) Evidence overreach independent of that conflict: both C3 findings are tagged [--] (unverified, not [OK]) and each is a single study — 'ignoring existing codebase' (12 of 24 tasks) supports a broad claim about agents not incorporating existing code/context, not specifically 'failed to reuse an existing helper before writing a new one'; the 19%-slower figure is about correcting output mismatches with codebase expectations, not about duplicate-file creation at all. The A3 'abstraction inversion' citation describes a different phenomenon — a deficient library/abstraction forcing its users to re-implement functionality the abstraction should have exposed — not an agent failing to search the codebase before adding a new file. The author's own caveat concedes this directly: 'Creating a new file specifically has no direct finding of its own in the corpus — it is folded in here as the same underlying shape ... not as an independently evidenced claim.' That is an invented shape-match (judgment), not a precautionary extrapolation from evidence that is at least on-topic. The reviewer test is also partly unfalsifiable in practice: its SATISFIES branch ('a search for an existing equivalent was made') cannot be verified from a diff alone and would require trusting the agent's self-report of having searched.
rules.reinstated_because: Corpus names a concrete signal; adjudicated 2026-09-11 after the tests-vs-tells distinction was drawn.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if an equivalent helper, utility, or established local pattern already exists in the codebase and the diff adds another without reusing it. SATISFIES if no equivalent exists, or the diff names why the existing one doesn't fit. Weaker than it looks: the SATISFIES branch cannot be verified from a diff alone when it rests on the author's report of having searched.

rules.text: When your own reply comes out longer or more hedge-dense than the question required, don't just cut it to length — the excess is a signal about a specific claim inside it, not just noise to prune. Re-check that claim. If you can confirm it, tighten the passage to the confident version. If you can't, keep the uncertainty as an explicit marker (e.g. "unconfirmed", "I haven't verified X") rather than smoothing it into prose that reads as confident.
rules.why:
Two independent, each-sufficient problems.

(1) Locked-decision violation. locked.md's Surfaces section is explicit: "The correctness gate has NO evidenced analogue outside code — say so explicitly, offer no substitute." Conversational output is one of the four non-code surfaces this applies to. P1B-1 nonetheless invents exactly such a substitute for the chat surface: it prescribes a verification procedure ("re-check that claim... confirm it... tighten... or keep the uncertainty marker") and a matching REVIEWER TEST with VIOLATES/SATISFIES criteria — the same shape as the universal code gate, transplanted onto a surface locked.md says gets none. Per the audit brief, a rule violating a locked decision is wrong regardless of merit.

(2) Evidence overread, matching the exploration's own challenge note on this exact direction (line 311, "15 · Length as a diagnostic"): "the cited chat literature mostly establishes that length is rewarded, which is a different claim from length signalling the model's own uncertainty." Of the three cited claims, only C1's verbosity-compensation finding (line 172) actually ties to uncertainty, and only at whole-response granularity — not to "a specific claim inside it." The RLHF r=0.451 (line 161) and the IFEval U-shaped brevity-failure finding (line 169) are about length being rewarded / brevity-compliance failing in aggregate, not about a reply signaling low confidence in one particular claim. The rule's "convergent mechanism evidence" framing folds these three together as if they agreed on the localized-signal claim; they don't. The localization move itself ("the excess is a signal about a specific claim inside it") is the exploration doc's own admitted extrapolation ("nothing in the 471-finding corpus tests preamble redundancy directly," line 259), and the direction's own falsification test — score flagged passages against known-wrong ground truth — was never run. Every backing claim carries [--] (unverified-quantitative), not [OK]. "Precautionary" implies convergence; two of the three citations don't actually converge on what the rule asserts.
rules.reinstated_because: Corpus names a concrete signal; adjudicated 2026-09-11 after the tests-vs-tells distinction was drawn.
rules.reviewer_test: diagnosis only — no reviewer test. This routes a flagged passage to verification or an explicit uncertainty marker; it does not yield a verdict on the draft.

rules.text:
A comment that restates the line immediately below it is a signal of unreviewed generation, not documentation. Removing it is subject to the same gate as any other deletion.
Falsification: the signal is a practitioner tell — the most-upvoted marker of AI-generated comments, recurring independently in a second thread — with no measured link to a defect or maintenance outcome. If restating comments turn out to correlate with no downstream harm, this is a style preference and should be dropped.
rules.reviewer_test: VIOLATES if a diff adds a comment whose content is fully recoverable from the line it precedes. SATISFIES otherwise.
rules.evidence: E3-reddit-docs: the single most-upvoted tell for AI-generated comments, recurring independently in a second unrelated thread; C3 over-commenting quality findings.
rules.audit_note: Added 2026-09-11 during rule-set adjudication, not produced by the drafting pass.

cut.text: Check whether the diff adds anything — an endpoint, a flag, a handled edge case, a generalized parameter — that the request didn't ask for and that isn't needed to fix the bug or satisfy the ask. Each addition should trace to something a reviewer could point to in the request.
cut.why:
Two independent, each-sufficient problems.

(1) LOCKED-DECISION VIOLATION. locked.md's Content rules state: "DETECTION: ship ONLY the two tests that survived adversarial scrutiny — (a) the co-evolution question for duplication... (b) the pruning test for rules... State plainly that the other surfaces are not checkable at review time." S3 is a third, unauthorized detection heuristic for surface-code (traceability of an added surface to the request). The exploration doc's own "detection is the weakest link" theme is explicit that this category has no review-time answer: "Over-engineering's only clean definition is retrospective... Nothing available at review time decides this" except the two named tests, and "Everything else in the smell catalogue requires human judgement." S3 resurrects exactly the kind of third mechanical-sounding test the locked scope was drawn to exclude. Per the task framing, this alone makes it wrong regardless of merit.

(2) EVIDENCE MISATTRIBUTION. The claimed-evidence parenthetical — "(peer, the Horikawa refactoring-instance study — D2-4 confirms this traces to a real academic source, distinct from the fragile N=20 preprint)" — does not survive a grep. D2-4's actual question list (line 558) covers LinearB's 67.3%, the 43%-vs-54.9% refactoring and 1.1%-vs-13.7% duplication figures, the 83% maintenance figure, the 9.9% deletion figure, assertion-roulette, and the 45%/70% security figures. It never mentions "scope creep" at all — that claim (line 212, C3-agent-failure-modes) was never traced to Horikawa or to any specific study by D2-4; it sits unflagged, uninvestigated. Separately, the Horikawa study D2-4 *did* investigate is tagged (prep) — an ACM TOSEM preprint, not peer-reviewed (line 562) — so calling it "peer" inverts the corpus's own source-type tag, and the caveat the author borrows ("D2-4 flags the refactoring study's human-comparator figures as reranked from a different corpus") is real but belongs to the 43%/54.9% statistic, not to the scope-creep claim it's attached to here. The author's own caveat honestly flags "none is a controlled study," which is right, but the "peer... confirms this traces to a real academic source" framing oversells a link the corpus does not establish.

Net: even setting aside the locked-decision violation, the remaining support collapses to three unflagged, non-adjudicated corpus lines (C3 "scope creep," A3 "gold plating... unexplained extras," and the Devin anecdote) — genuinely convergent in shape, transferring cleanly to coding agents, but never run through the challenge process the other 15 directions went through, and explicitly named by the exploration doc as belonging to the "requires human judgement" bucket rather than the two tests licensed for shipping.

cut.text: A new interface, base class, plugin or strategy layer, or wrapper that has exactly one concrete implementation, and nothing in the task names or implies a second, is a signal worth a second look — not proof of over-engineering.
cut.why:
Two independent problems, either one sufficient to cut.

(1) Locked-decision violation (decisive on its own). The locked DETECTION rule says "ship ONLY the two tests that survived adversarial scrutiny" — the co-evolution test for duplication and the pruning test for rules — and explicitly forbids shipping other structural/countable code metrics as over-engineering signals ("Do NOT ship cyclomatic thresholds, method-size limits, dead-code rates, or cohesion metrics — these specifically failed verification"). S4's REVIEWER TEST ("search for implementers... returns exactly one and no second is named") is a third mechanical, reviewer-executable check of exactly that rejected shape — count a structural property, flag on a threshold (here, count=1). It doesn't matter that S4 hedges the verdict as "worth a second look, not proof": the locked constraint bars shipping the checkable apparatus itself, not just strong claims built on it. S4 is also the direct descendant of exploration-doc direction 12 ("trace content to a named consumer"), which the corpus's own challenge notes found "oversells the machinery by citing the clone co-evolution test as a validated model when the corpus's own reading of that test is far weaker," and which sits in an explicitly "Irreducible" block-vs-log tension with direction 3 that "the corpus does not adjudicate." The DETECTION lock reads as the design's resolution of that exact unresolved territory — by excluding it, not by admitting a softened version of it under a different section label.

(2) Even setting the lock aside, the evidence cited doesn't support the specific mechanical test chosen. The CLAIMED EVIDENCE leans on C3's "abstraction excess" and the Devin case study — both unmarked practitioner anecdotes (one N=1 case study) about abstracting "for imaginary scale" / "non-existent problems" — and A3's rule-of-three folk wisdom, which is about deferring DRY-driven abstraction from repeated code, not about counting implementers of an interface. None of these establishes that "exactly one concrete implementation, no second named in the task" is itself the tell. The corpus's actual best-supported claim on this exact question — A3, line 54: "(book) Speculative generality can be detected when the only users of a function or class are test cases," reinforced by the exploration doc's own statement that this is "the" one mechanical tell that survives (line 80) — is narrower and different: it requires the abstraction have no real caller at all, not merely one implementation. S4's chosen test is broader than what even the corpus's strongest source licenses, and on a real (non-cherry-picked) draft — a dependency-injection interface with a single implementation but many live production callers, no prior similar seam in the codebase — it would read VIOLATES-leaning for code that isn't speculative generality by the corpus's own definition.

cut.text: When two rules in the same agent-facing doc conflict, delete or merge one of them. Never resolve the conflict by ranking them — adding precedence language ('rule A overrides rule B'), relying on file order to imply priority, or leaving both live with a disambiguating note.
cut.why:
The cited evidence (claims.txt line 122, B1-agent-docs) says only that Anthropic's docs report contradictory CLAUDE.md/rules content gets resolved *arbitrarily* today, with "no defined precedence rule," and that Anthropic's own recommended remedy is "periodic manual audit" — nothing more specific. That evidence supports "conflicts should be audited"; it does not say what the audit's fix should be, and it never mentions precedence language, let alone tests whether adding it (e.g. "rule A overrides rule B") fails to resolve the arbitrariness. D3 inverts the gap: it invents delete-or-merge as the *only* legal remedy and explicitly bans precedence annotation — the one technique that would directly patch the exact defect the source names (absence of a defined precedence rule). That's check #1's overreading failure: an inference that reverses its source.

It also ignores the corpus's most directly on-point data: D1-4's own controlled factorial study (arXiv 2605.10039) manipulated "the presence of a directly conflicting instruction" as a structural variable and found no detectable compliance effect from it. Whatever its caveats (single-author preprint, trivial marker, single-turn harness — noted honestly in the exploration doc), it is the only empirical test of this exact question in the corpus, and it points toward "conflicting rules aren't shown to matter much," not toward "conflicts are dangerous enough to mandate deletion." The exploration doc's own synthesis states this question was left open — "Nothing resolves conflicts when several directions fire on the same draft... no direction supplies precedence" — meaning the source material explicitly declined to adjudicate delete/merge vs. precedence-language, yet D3 asserts a confident, mandatory answer the corpus never reached.

Enacting D3 also risks the exact harm the corpus flags elsewhere ("simplicity pressure without a correctness anchor destroys function"): forced deletion/merging on any spotted contradiction, with the non-destructive fix (precedence annotation) categorically forbidden, assumes an editor can always correctly judge which of two rules is simply wrong — but many real "conflicts" are actually two rules each correct in different contexts, where precedence or scoping is the safer fix and deletion is the one that loses information.

cut.text: A sentence narrating a tool call must add a fact the visible tool output doesn't already show — an inference, a decision, or a consequence. If it only restates what the output already displays, cut it.
cut.why:
Locked-decision violation, independent of evidence quality. The "Content rules → DETECTION" bullet in locked.md is explicit and total: "ship ONLY the two tests that survived adversarial scrutiny — (a) the co-evolution question for duplication... (b) the pruning test for rules... State plainly that the other surfaces are not checkable at review time." P1B-3 is a third, bespoke checkable detection test — a Part-1 "spot over-production, then cut" mechanism (matches the two-job model exactly: detect redundancy, prescribe cutting it) — invented specifically for the surface-chat surface. That is precisely the move the locked decision forbids: conversational output is one of "the other surfaces" the design says must be *disclosed* as not checkable, not given its own replacement heuristic. The rule's good evidentiary hygiene doesn't rescue it — this is a scope/structure violation, and locked.md says such a rule "is wrong regardless of merit."

On the merits, for the record: the rule doesn't overclaim. Both the claimed-evidence field and the author's caveat already disclose, correctly, that the narration clause is "this landscape's own extrapolation" with "nothing in the 471-finding corpus test[ing] preamble or recap redundancy directly" — confirmed by grepping the exploration doc, where this exact sentence appears three times (lines 259, 344, and in the "what the landscape does not reach" list). The direction-15 challenge note's falsification test targets the *other* half of direction 15 (length/hedge-density as a confidence signal), not the narration clause — so the narration clause was never even falsification-tested, consistent with "untested" and with tagging it the weakest of the three status tiers (judgment). No [!!] claims, no blocklisted figures, no magnitude. The reviewer test itself is mechanically workable on a real transcript (e.g. narration restating a git-status file list VIOLATES; narration naming which file it'll act on next and why SATISFIES). None of that matters, though, against the locked cap on how many checkable detection tests this skill may ship, and against the explicit instruction to state chat as non-checkable rather than patch that gap with an untested, author-invented heuristic.

cut.text: This skill obeys its own gate: every rule below carries a status tag and either a reviewer test or an explicit diagnosis-only label, the file stays under the line budget, and no rule outside the blocklist's quoted examples states a number.
cut.why: Fails the skill's own pruning test (locked.md line 22: "would removing this cause a mistake? Actually remove the candidate and observe"). Remove M7 from the draft and check: every other rule still carries its status tag, still has its reviewer test or diagnosis-only label, the file is still free of stray magnitudes, the line budget still binds — because those four properties are enforced by the process that assembles and audits SKILL.md (this very review), not by the file asserting them about itself. M7 does no guidance work; it restates constraints that already bind by construction. It also has no home in the design: the tiered budget (locked.md 9-11) reserves the always-on core for "the gate + the two surviving tests," and M7 is neither and fits none of the five surfaces (29-31), so under the activation model it has no slot to earn. Separately, the reviewer test's carve-out ("no rule outside the blocklist's quoted examples states a number") is a defensible reconciliation of two locked clauses but is not itself present in locked.md, which states the no-magnitudes rule unqualified (line 24) — CLAIMED EVIDENCE cites the unqualified source for a qualified rule. That drift is minor standing alone but confirms M7 is doing design work under the guise of restating a locked decision. If the four checks are worth keeping, they belong in the build/audit checklist that produces SKILL.md or in the companion doc, not as a numbered rule competing for the file's tight line budget.

assembly.budget_note:
Core is 5 active checks (G1 sequencing, G2 symmetry, G3 decision-authority, D1-coevolution, D2-pruning-executed) plus 2 stated-once framing lines whose checks apply when guidance is authored rather than per change: G4 (no correctness-check analogue outside code) and D3-retrospective-only (no detector beyond D1/D2 anywhere else). Both framing lines belong in core rather than restated per surface, because locked.md line 8 bars restating the gate per surface — D3 is the Part-1 twin of that instruction and earns the same one-shot placement. Five surface-local copies of "this isn't a gate" would itself be the duplication this skill teaches reviewers to catch.

Per-surface counts, on the 5-active-core convention: code 6 → 11 · specs 3 → 8 · agent-facing docs 4 → 9 · human-facing docs 4 → 9 · conversational output 2 → 7. A task touching exactly one surface therefore faces 7–11 simultaneous constraints, worst at code. That still satisfies locked.md's "no single task faces all rules" bar, but it is not the "genuinely small" number this note claimed before the reinstatement of S2(code), S6(code) and P1B-1(chat) — and code, the modal surface, is the worst case. Meta (M1–M6) mostly doesn't add to that count: M2/M4/M5 are declarative (precedence, claims scope, harness boundary), not per-draft checks; M1/M3/M6 are conditionally triggered (citing evidence, writing a deletion rationale, dispatching a subagent), not live on every firing.

The tiering is weaker for the very common case of a task spanning two surfaces at once — implementing a spec'd change touches code AND the spec that authorized it; editing a workflow governed by a CLAUDE.md touches agent-docs AND code. Nothing in the tiering caps cross-surface stacking: core(5) + code(6) + specs(3) = 14 checks, or core(5) + code(6) + agent-docs(4) = 15. Compliance is reported to degrade as simultaneous constraints accumulate (per this skill's own premise), so the honest verdict is: defensible for genuinely single-surface work, not proven for the multi-surface case that is arguably the modal one, and locked.md sets no cross-surface cap to fall back on. These counts are for this audit only — locked.md's "NO MAGNITUDES" rule bans any of these numbers from appearing in the shipped SKILL.md body; only directional language ("compliance falls as constraints accumulate") may ship.
assembly.duplication_found:
Applying the skill's own co-evolution test (D1-coevolution: would the two regions need to change together?) to the assembled rule set itself:

1. HD4's reviewer test is a repackaging of HD2 + HD3, not new content. HD4's SATISFIES clause ("the stated justification is a system-of-record duplicate") restates HD2's "default to reducing to a pointer... system of record acceptable grounds to consolidate," and HD4's override clause ("contract/SLA/compliance obligation overrides that ground") restates HD3's "judged against that obligation, not traffic." Edit HD2's default-to-pointer logic or HD3's override logic, and HD4's VIOLATES/SATISFIES test breaks unless edited in lockstep. Three rules encoding two pieces of substance.

2. M1's blocklist entry for "McCabe's tiered cyclomatic-complexity risk scale" (and its dead-code-prevalence entry) duplicates D4-blocklist-metrics' banned list and CLAIMED EVIDENCE text — both bans rest on the identical underlying verification fact (McCabe's paper offers one number, called a personal judgment call, not a validated scale; the dead-code figure traces to one vendor's own estimate). A later correction to the McCabe or dead-code finding has to be made in both M1 and D4-blocklist-metrics or the two rules go out of sync.

3. Inside the always-on core itself: G3's VIOLATES clause ("...accepted on the grounds that it's simpler while the correctness check... was never run") restates G1's re-run-after-simplification requirement as part of G3's own test. A change to G1's re-run condition (e.g., what counts as "re-run") forces a matching edit to G3's test — and this pair sits in the core, where every line is paid on every single firing, so the redundancy is costlier there than elsewhere.

Checked and ruled OUT as duplication (the deliberately-independent case D1-coevolution itself carves out): D2(agentdocs) ("check for an existing rule covering substantially the same ground") and D1-coevolution ("do these two regions require synchronized change?") look parallel — both detect overlap — but they apply to different regions (agent-doc rule text vs. general code/duplication) with no shared requirement forcing synchronized edits between them. Not a duplication finding; flagged instead under gaps as a consistency question, because S6 (a same-shape duplicate-detector for code helpers) was cut for violating locked.md's one-operationalizable-detector restriction and D2(agentdocs) was not.
gaps: Diagnosis-not-enforcement labeling: locked.md's hard constraint requires every rule that can't yield a VIOLATES/SATISFIES verdict to be either cut or explicitly labeled diagnosis-not-enforcement. D3-retrospective-only, S2(specs), S3(specs), and D5(agentdocs) all carry that label; S1(surface-code) and P1B-2 both have reviewer_test_holds=false with no such label attached in the surviving text — as drafted they violate the hard constraint and need the label added or need cutting.

Falsification one-liners: locked.md requires them inline, but only G1 actually carries one in the surviving set. G3, D1-coevolution, S1(code), S5, D1(agentdocs), D5(agentdocs), S1(specs), S3(specs), and M4 are all precautionary without a matching falsification line — these still need to be drafted, not assumed present from the audit.

Budget hygiene against the 500-line hard cap: D4-blocklist-metrics' replacement CLAIMED EVIDENCE paragraph and AUTHOR'S CAVEAT, plus M1's parenthetical per-claim explanations, are exactly the justification/provenance prose that locked.md's Disclosure section says belongs in a companion reference file, not inline in SKILL.md. As currently specified these two rules are the biggest line-cost items against the budget and need to be split into a one-line ban + one-line falsification inline, with the evidence paragraph moved to the companion doc.

Planning-time vs. code-time activation: locked.md's Activation section requires the skill to 'fire at planning time AND code time, with different rules at each.' Nothing in the surviving rule set or this tiering carries that axis — every rule here is organized purely by content-surface. The final assembly needs to decide which of these rules apply at plan time, which at code time, and which at both; that decision isn't represented anywhere yet.

Code-surface over-production detection is nearly empty after the audit's cuts. S2, S3, S4, and S6 — the rules that named concrete over-production patterns (uncalled new functions/parameters, new endpoints/flags/edge cases, single-implementation interface layers, redundant helpers) — were all cut for violating the locked one-detector-per-kind restriction. What remains for code is S1 (judge at diff-level, not function-level) and S5 (new config flag is a signal) — both modifiers on how to look, not what to look for. Locked.md's Part 1 job ('spot over-production') has little content left for its primary surface; this is a direct consequence of the audit's cuts, not an oversight in this assembly pass, but it should be flagged before shipping rather than discovered later.

Conversational-output surface is thin to the point of tokenism. Locked.md's Surfaces section states 'all five carry rules,' but after P1B-1 (overall verbosity/hedge-density) and P1B-3 (tool-call narration) were cut, only P1B-2 (don't repeat the same hedge twice) survives — a single narrow rule, next to core's generic framing. It technically satisfies 'carries a rule' but not the apparent intent of five comparably-weighted surfaces.

Consistency gap on duplication detectors: D2(agentdocs) survived as an overlap/duplication check for agent-facing docs while S6, a same-shape duplicate-detector for code helpers, was cut for violating locked.md's restriction to exactly one operationalizable duplication test (D1-coevolution). Nothing in the surviving material states why the agent-docs case is exempt from the restriction that killed the code case — needs either a stated rationale (agent-doc overlap-checking is an application of D1-coevolution's co-evolution question, not a second detector) or D2(agentdocs) should be cut on the same grounds as S6.

ID collisions across sections (S1 used in both surface-code and surface-specs; D1/D2/D3/D4 used in both the 'tests' section and surface-agentdocs) are not resolved anywhere in the surviving-rules material itself — this assembly disambiguates them as S1(code)/S1(specs) and D1(agentdocs)/D2(agentdocs)/etc., but that renaming needs to actually land in the shipped SKILL.md, not stay implicit.

Locked.md's Activation section also requires 'narrow triggers, not always-on' and an explicit 'supersedes applying-simplicity-principles' statement — these are SKILL.md frontmatter/description concerns with no corresponding rule ID in the surviving set, so the rule-level audit never covered them and this tiering can't surface them as rule_ids; they need to be handled directly when the file is authored.
gap_status: gap 1 (diagnosis-not-enforcement labelling): RESOLVED. S1(code) is diagnosis-only and logic.md now says so. P1B-2(chat)'s test does hold and is flagged true; P1B-1(chat) carries the diagnosis-only line it lacked. G4 is not diagnosis-only — its test holds on authored guidance — and budget_note no longer calls it a zero-check line; it is a stated-once line whose check applies when guidance is written, which is a statement about cost per firing, not enforceability.

gap 2 (falsification one-liners inline): RESOLVED. Every precautionary rule now carries one, drawn from its own evidence field. S2(code) and S6(code) carry the honest version instead — no falsifying test exists in the corpus, and they were reinstated on the rationale that the corpus names the signal, not on a measured result. D4-blocklist-metrics also carries one although it is grounded, because its ban rests on misattribution rather than on a positive result and can therefore lapse per metric; the other three grounded rules carry none.
gap 3 (budget hygiene for D4-blocklist-metrics and M1): OPEN — split to a one-line ban plus falsification inline when the file is authored.

gap 4 (plan-time vs code-time activation): RESOLVED. The surface in play identifies the moment — writing a spec is plan time, writing code is code time, a doc or a reply is whenever that artifact is authored — and the core fires at every moment. No rule is time-gated independently of its surface. Stated in logic.md's Data flow and amended into the locked decision.
gap 5 (code-surface detection nearly empty): partly resolved — S2(code) and S6(code) were reinstated, taking code from 2 rules to 6.
gap 6 (conversational surface thin to the point of tokenism): partly resolved — P1B-1(chat) was reinstated, taking the surface from 1 rule to 2.

gap 7 (agent-docs duplication detector exempt from the restriction that cut S6): the asymmetry it complained of is gone — S6(code) is live again. The question it raised is not answered: nothing yet states why D2(agentdocs) is an overlap check rather than a second duplication detector competing with D1-coevolution. OPEN as a rationale gap.
gap 8 (id collisions unresolved in the shipped material): resolved — ids are qualified in rules[] and cut[] on the assembly convention.
gap 9 (frontmatter-level activation concerns have no rule id): OPEN — handle when the file is authored.

assembly.duplication_found (the three co-evolution failures in the rule set itself): RESOLVED. Item 1 — HD4's restatement of HD2's system-of-record ground and HD3's obligation override — cut from HD4's text and reviewer test. Item 2 — M1 and D4-blocklist-metrics both carrying the McCabe and dead-code verification facts — resolved by D4's evidence pointing at M1 rather than restating them; D4 bans using the metrics, M1 bans citing the failed claims. Item 3 — G3's reviewer test restating G1's re-run requirement inside the core — cut from G3's test.
post_audit_corrections: Ids qualified with their section (S1(code)/S1(specs), S2(code)/S2(specs), D1..D5(agentdocs), P1B-1/2(chat), and the cut entries) so every id in rules[] and cut[] is unique. The assembly block already used this convention; rules[] and cut[] did not.

Drafting scaffold ('ID:', 'SECTION:', 'TEXT:', 'STATUS:', "AUTHOR'S STATUS:", 'REVIEWER TEST:', 'CLAIMED EVIDENCE:') stripped from the text of G2, G3, D2(agentdocs), D5(agentdocs), M6 and P1B-2(chat), where it had leaked into the shipped payload.

Where a rule's text carried an embedded REVIEWER TEST that disagreed with its reviewer_test field, the embedded (post-audit) version was promoted and the field discarded as a stale draft — D2(agentdocs), D5(agentdocs), M6, P1B-2(chat). In every case the field version contradicted the rule's own body: D2's imposed a rule-count cap the body does not ask for; D5's prescribed re-assertion at a dispatch point, the remedy the body explicitly refuses to assume and the audit had already ruled unevidenced; M6's referred to 'the gate's two tests', conflating the gate with the two detection tests; P1B-2's flagged the separate-risk caveat its body carves out. G3's two versions were semantically identical and the field's prose was kept.
P1B-2(chat) reviewer_test_holds corrected false -> true (it carries a working VIOLATES/SATISFIES pair); P1B-1(chat) given the diagnosis-only reviewer_test and reviewer_test_holds=false it lacked.
assembly.always_on_core, assembly.per_surface and stats regenerated from rules[]; budget_note arithmetic re-derived. All three were pre-reinstatement snapshots.

D4-blocklist-metrics' text field held the auditor's editing memo rather than a rule. The rule was written from the memo's instructions and the surviving reviewer test; the memo's corrected evidence paragraph replaced the old one, which carried the Shepperd/Landman overread the audit had flagged.
HD4's embedded 'Reviewer test:' block removed (lower-case, so the first scaffold pass missed it).

Every precautionary rule given a falsification line. S2(code) and S6(code) given reviewer tests and reviewer_test_holds=true; S6's records inside the test that its SATISFIES branch is weaker, since it can rest on the author's report of having searched.
The three duplication failures the audit recorded against the rule set itself were merged out rather than disclosed — see gap_status.
S7(code)'s trailing precedence clause removed; M2 states precedence once and a surface rule restating it is the shape this spec bars for the gate.

stats.note: Every count here is derived from rules[] and cut[]. The previous drafted/kept/cut totals (36/28/8) did not reconcile with those lists — 36 − 8 + 4 reinstated = 32 final leaves 4 cut, but cut[] holds 5 — and its status_tally was a pre-reinstatement snapshot carrying a malformed key. The drafting history could not be reconstructed from the asset, so it was dropped rather than reconciled by guess. `audited` counts rules carrying a full audit record (reviewer test + evidence); of those, `audit_note_empty` passed the audit without a recorded note. The 3 rules reinstated on rationale alone — S2(code), S6(code), P1B-1(chat) — carry `why` and `reinstated_because` in place of an audit record, so the asset holds no evidence or auditor's note for them. Their reviewer tests were written during the review pass, not by the audit.
